This gestational duration is consistent with that of other medium-sized Neotoma species, reflecting a typical eutherian reproductive schedule. The pre-weaning interval is relatively brief, with nutritional independence from the mother occurring through weaning at 26 days after birth [tx = 26 days after birth] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. During the suckling juvenile stage, pups transition from milk to solid food, and the wet weight at the moment of weaning is recorded as 35.6 grams [Wwx = 35.6 grams], indicating substantial growth during the neonatal and pre-weaning phases.

Female Southern Plains woodrats attain puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive viability, at 136 days after birth [tp = 136 days after birth], a value documented in a controlled environment at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The ultimate or asymptotic adult body mass of the Southern Plains woodrat is 236.3 grams [Wwi = 236.3 grams], a value that represents the maximum wet weight typically attained by fully mature, reproductively viable individuals. This mass is characteristic of a medium-sized Neotoma, placing it between the smaller Neotoma floridana and the larger Neotoma cinerea. In the field, individuals often exhibit some variation around this asymptote depending on local habitat quality and resource availability, but the maximum recorded mass from extensive trapping surveys and museum specimen series consistently converges near this figure. The growth trajectory from the neonatal mass of 11.7 grams [Wwb = 11.7 grams] to this adult size represents a roughly twenty-fold increase, a pattern typical of altricial cricetids investing heavily in early postnatal development. This period of rapid mass gain during the suckling and juvenile stages is followed by a gradual deceleration as the animal approaches its final structural dimensions, a pattern of somatic growth typical of eutherian mammals, with the most intense growth occurring in the first several months of life before the individual transitions into its post-pubertal, breeding adult stage.

The maximum recorded longevity figure nevertheless provides an upper bound on the species' potential life history, comparable to that of other cricetid rodents of similar body size. Reproductive output is therefore spread across multiple years, with the annual reproductive rate of 2.4 litters per year [F_R_i = 2.4 litters per year] contributing to overall lifetime fitness.

These nests serve as critical refugia for thermoregulation, buffering extreme temperature fluctuations that can exceed 40 °C in summer and fall below freezing in winter. The species exhibits a largely nocturnal activity pattern, which reduces exposure to diurnal heat and desiccation.
